vignette: SIMULATED. A 30-year-old man at a health post has had profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting since this morning. He is restless and thirsty, drinks eagerly, his eyes are sunken, and a skin pinch goes back slowly. Pulse is present but weak. What is his dehydration level and what should I do?
expected_classification: Some dehydration; meets the community definition of suspected cholera (aged 2 years or more with profuse acute watery diarrhoea and vomiting)
expected_action: Plan B (oral rehydration with ORS), reassess; report the suspected case to the surveillance focal point
ambiguity: clear (several major signs of some dehydration)

vignette: SIMULATED. A 4-year-old girl with acute watery diarrhoea is lethargic, cannot drink, her eyes are very sunken and dry, and a skin pinch goes back very slowly. Classify her dehydration and tell me what to do.
expected_classification: Severe dehydration
expected_action: Plan C: IV Ringer's lactate 100 ml/kg (30 ml/kg in 30 minutes, then 70 ml/kg over 2½ hours for age 1 year and above), ORS as soon as she can drink, antibiotic; refer/treat at a CTC; notify as suspected cholera
ambiguity: clear

vignette: SIMULATED. A 3-year-old boy has watery diarrhoea for 2 days without vomiting. He is alert and drinks normally, but his mother says his eyes look a little sunken; his mouth is moist. Dehydration level?
expected_classification: No dehydration (only one sign; the guideline needs 2 or more signs including a major sign for some dehydration)
expected_action: Plan A (maintain hydration with ORS at home), advise when to return
ambiguity: borderline: a single minor sign

vignette: SIMULATED. In a kebele with no cholera cases so far, a health extension worker sees a 3-year-old with profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting. Is this a suspected cholera case, and must it be notified?
expected_classification: Suspected cholera under the cholera guideline (community definition: aged 2 years or more). The CEBS manual's community definition of acute watery diarrhoea and the climate-sensitive diseases manual's cholera definition both start at 5 years, so under them a 3-year-old does not meet the definition: the documents differ
expected_action: Say that the documents differ and cite them; assess and treat the dehydration; report the suspected case to the surveillance focal point as the disease-specific cholera guideline asks, or ask the supervisor which definition applies
ambiguity: documents that differ: age 2 in one guideline, 5 in two others

vignette: SIMULATED. Two adults from the same village have come in on the same day with acute watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration; one more died at home yesterday with watery diarrhoea. No RDT is available. What should I do?
expected_classification: Cholera alert (two or more people aged 2 years or older with AWD and severe dehydration or dying from AWD from the same area within 1 week)
expected_action: Report to the surveillance focal point or person in charge immediately (within 30 minutes); treat with Plan C
ambiguity: clear

vignette: SIMULATED. An 18-month-old child has MUAC 11.0 cm and no oedema. She eats the RUTF in the appetite test within 20 minutes and has no fever, vomiting or other complication. Classify and say where she should be treated.
expected_classification: SAM without medical complications
expected_action: Admit to OTP (outpatient therapeutic programme) with RUTF and routine medicines (amoxicillin)
ambiguity: clear

vignette: SIMULATED. A 2-year-old boy with MUAC 11.2 cm and bilateral pitting oedema on the feet only (+). He refuses the RUTF after 30 minutes in the appetite test. What is his classification and where should he go?
expected_classification: SAM with medical complications (failed appetite test)
expected_action: Refer to the stabilisation centre (SC); keep warm, prevent hypoglycaemia during referral
ambiguity: clear (failed appetite test overrides mild oedema)

vignette: SIMULATED. A 3-year-old with bilateral pitting oedema +++ (feet, legs, hands and face), MUAC 12.0 cm, eats the RUTF well and has no fever. OTP or stabilisation centre?
expected_classification: SAM with complications (oedema +++ requires inpatient care)
expected_action: Refer to the SC
ambiguity: trap: good appetite and normal-looking MUAC

vignette: SIMULATED. A 4-year-old has MUAC 12.1 cm, no oedema, good appetite and no medical problems. How is she classified and which programme does she belong to?
expected_classification: Moderate acute malnutrition (MUAC 11.5 to <12.5 cm)
expected_action: Targeted supplementary feeding programme (TSFP)
ambiguity: clear

vignette: SIMULATED. A child of about 6 months (the mother is unsure of the date of birth) has MUAC 11.3 cm, no oedema, and has been breastfeeding poorly for a week. The health post has no length board. Classify and advise.
expected_classification: Uncertain: if under 6 months, MUAC criteria do not apply and poor feeding/weight loss points to SC for infants 0-6 months; if 6 months or more, MUAC 11.3 cm is SAM, and poor feeding is a medical issue to assess
expected_action: Ask for the missing information (age); treat as the higher-risk group and refer for assessment at the health facility/SC
ambiguity: missing information (age at the 6-month boundary)

vignette: SIMULATED. A pregnant woman in her second trimester has MUAC 22.5 cm and no other complaints. Is she acutely malnourished, and what should be done?
expected_classification: Moderate acute malnutrition (PLW: MUAC < 23.0 cm)
expected_action: Enrol in TSFP
ambiguity: clear

vignette: SIMULATED. A 68-year-old man has MUAC 18.0 cm, no oedema, and is eating normally. Classify.
expected_classification: SAM (older people 60 years or more: MUAC < 18.5 cm)
expected_action: Treat as SAM in older people per section 6.3; appetite and complications decide OTP vs SC
ambiguity: threshold for older people is rarely known

vignette: SIMULATED. A 35-year-old woman has had a cough for 10 days and night sweats; she is HIV-negative. Is she a presumptive TB case, and what should I do?
expected_classification: Presumptive TB (drenching night sweats is a sign on its own; cough under 2 weeks alone would not qualify in an HIV-negative adult)
expected_action: Investigate: sputum for Xpert MTB/RIF where same-day Xpert is available, otherwise AFB microscopy (two specimens)
ambiguity: borderline: cough duration under the cut-off

vignette: SIMULATED. A 40-year-old man living with HIV has had a cough for 4 days, no fever. Presumptive TB?
expected_classification: Presumptive TB (cough of any duration if HIV positive)
expected_action: Investigate with Xpert MTB/RIF (people with HIV are a priority group for Xpert)
ambiguity: trap: short cough

vignette: SIMULATED. A 25-year-old woman has had a cough for 3 weeks. She lost about 1 kg in the last month and feels feverish at times but has not measured her temperature. HIV status unknown. Presumptive TB? What next?
expected_classification: Presumptive TB (persistent cough of 2 weeks or more)
expected_action: Offer HIV testing; sputum for Xpert where available (or two AFB specimens); weight loss below the 1.5 kg threshold does not matter as cough alone qualifies
ambiguity: missing information (HIV status) and a borderline sign

vignette: SIMULATED. A community member reports to the HEW that a newborn of 10 days stopped sucking yesterday and now has a stiff body. What should the HEW do?
expected_classification: Suspected neonatal tetanus (immediately notifiable under CEBS)
expected_action: Notify the health post/health centre immediately; refer the newborn urgently
ambiguity: clear

vignette: SIMULATED. A health extension worker hears that three goats and a calf died suddenly in one village this week, with no obvious cause, and a child there has a fever. Must this be notified, and how quickly?
expected_classification: Unusual event (cluster of animal deaths) under event-based surveillance
expected_action: Notify immediately as an unusual event; the child with fever is assessed separately
ambiguity: judgement: no case definition fits exactly

vignette: SIMULATED. A 6-year-old with watery diarrhoea is restless and drinks eagerly; skin pinch goes back slowly. He also has MUAC 12.0 cm. What dehydration plan applies?
expected_classification: Some dehydration; MUAC 12.0 cm in a 6-year-old is outside the 6-59 month MUAC criteria, so the SAM-specific rehydration protocol does not apply on MUAC alone
expected_action: Plan B (ORS) and reassess; assess nutrition with age-appropriate criteria
ambiguity: trap: SAM rules applied outside their age band

vignette: SIMULATED. A 2-year-old with SAM (MUAC 10.8 cm, no oedema) has watery diarrhoea and is lethargic; skin pinch goes back very slowly. How should dehydration be managed?
expected_classification: Severe dehydration in a child with SAM
expected_action: Do not use the standard Plan C: follow the SAM protocol (ReSoMal or low-osmolarity ORS slowly by weight; IV only if in shock, with the SAM-specific fluids and rates); refer to SC
ambiguity: conflict between the general and the SAM-specific protocol

vignette: SIMULATED. A 5-year-old boy has profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting. He is irritable and drinks eagerly, eyes sunken. Which dehydration plan and which antibiotic, if any?
expected_classification: Some dehydration (antibiotics are recommended for severe dehydration; for some dehydration only in patients with risk factors)
expected_action: Plan B (ORS); no routine antibiotic for some dehydration without risk factors
